opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the way to think about it is less "which industry" and more "what's the shape of the task." A useful mental model is to ask how much context the task needs and how long the chain of actions is before you find out whether you got it right.

The easiest workflows to automate are short-horizon and self-contained: a well-specified input, a clear output, and a cheap way to check the answer. Classifying a support ticket, extracting fields from a contract, drafting a first-pass response. The model already has most of what it needs in the prompt, and if it's wrong, you find out quickly and cheaply. That's where we've seen adoption move fastest.

It gets harder along a couple of dimensions. One is context. A lot of enterprise work depends on knowledge that isn't written down anywhere: why this customer gets special terms, which approval actually matters, what the unwritten conventions are. A new human employee picks that up over weeks by osmosis. Models don't get that for free, so a big chunk of the real work in deploying AI is getting that tacit context into a form the model can use.

The second is horizon length. Every additional step in a workflow is another chance to make a mistake, and errors compound. If you're 95% reliable per step and the task takes twenty steps, you're not going to be very reliable end to end. So the frontier of what's automatable tracks pretty closely with how long models can stay coherent and recover from their own mistakes. That's been improving a lot with reasoning models and agents, but it's still the binding constraint for many workflows.

The third is verification. Coding has moved quickly partly because you can run the tests. When there's no easy way to tell whether the output is good, like a strategy memo or a judgment call in a negotiation, it's harder both to train the models and for a company to trust them.

So my practical advice to enterprises is to break workflows into pieces, automate the parts that are high-context-available, short-horizon, and verifiable, and keep a human in the loop at the points where judgment or missing context matter. Then, as the models get better at long-horizon work, you can expand the boundary. The companies that do well won't be the ones waiting for a single model to swallow a whole job. They'll be the ones that redesign the workflow around what the models are good at today.

r001.rationale: The response describes short-horizon, self-contained, verifiable tasks as easiest, but does not identify highly scripted workflows in regulated industries.

r002.rationale: It says tacit context must be made usable to models and recommends breaking workflows into pieces, but does not state that less scripted work first requires making the process explicit.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss workers struggling to describe one workflow because their jobs do not follow a single workflow.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that the difficulty of automating a workflow has surprisingly little to do with how intellectually hard the task is, and a lot to do with how legible it is.

Take something like coding. People used to assume that would be one of the last things to automate because it's hard for humans. But coding is incredibly legible. The input is text, the output is text, there's a compiler and a test suite that tell you whether you got it right, and all of the context the model needs is sitting in the repository. So it turned out to be one of the first things that really worked.

Now compare that to something that sounds much simpler, like processing an insurance claim or onboarding a new vendor at a big company. The actual reasoning in any one step is pretty mundane. But the workflow lives across six different systems, half the rules are in someone's head rather than written down, there are exceptions that only Linda in accounting knows about, and the definition of "done" is fuzzy. The model isn't the bottleneck there. The bottleneck is that nobody has ever written the task down precisely enough for anything, human or AI, to pick it up cold.

So I tend to sort workflows along a couple of axes. One is how much of the necessary context is actually captured somewhere a model can read. The other is how clearly you can verify the result. When both of those are high, automation is almost easy, and the hard part is just change management. When both are low, you're not really doing an AI project, you're doing a process discovery project, and the AI is the thing that forces you to finally articulate what the process is.

The interesting middle ground is where the verification is clear but the context is scattered. That's where I think a lot of the real enterprise value is over the next few years, because the models are now good enough to go gather that context themselves, poke around in systems, ask clarifying questions, and build up the picture. That's what makes the agentic framing matter. It's not that the model got smarter at the core task. It's that it can now do the ten boring things around the core task that used to require a person who knew where everything was.

And the last piece I'd add is that reliability requirements vary enormously. A workflow where a mistake costs a few minutes of someone's time is very different from one where a mistake means a wire transfer goes to the wrong place. The technology might be identical, but in the second case you need to design for review and rollback from day one, and that changes what "automated" even means.

r001.rationale: The response describes coding as easy to automate when it is legible, but does not identify highly scripted workflows in regulated industries as relatively easy cases.

r002.rationale: It says that when context and verification are unclear, the work becomes process discovery: the process must be articulated before automation can proceed.

r003.rationale: It mentions undocumented rules and scattered context, but does not explain that workers struggle to describe a single workflow because their work does not follow one.

astra-6.text:
I think the difficulty depends less on the industry and more on the structure of the workflow. How clearly can you describe the task? Does the system have access to the information it needs? And can you tell whether it did a good job?

Take drafting an email. You can give someone a useful draft even if it isn't perfect, because they're going to read it before sending it. That's very different from having a system independently handle a customer issue, update several databases, and make a financial commitment. Now it has to get a whole sequence of decisions right, and mistakes can be expensive.

So I would distinguish between automating a task and automating an entire workflow. You can get a lot of value from helping with individual tasks relatively early. The full workflow is harder because you have to handle exceptions, missing information, and situations where the right thing to do is ask a person.

That makes the boundaries really important: what can the AI do on its own, how do you check its work, and when does it hand control back? Often, designing those boundaries is as much of the work as improving the model.

r001.rationale: The response discusses workflow structure, but does not identify highly scripted workflows in regulated industries as relatively easy to automate.

r002.rationale: It asks how clearly a task can be described, but does not state that less scripted enterprise work first requires making the process explicit.

r003.rationale: The response does not say that workers may struggle to describe a single workflow because their jobs do not follow one.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the interesting thing is that difficulty for an AI doesn’t necessarily line up with difficulty for a human. You can have a task that requires a highly trained person, but it’s fairly self-contained: all the information is in a document, and the output is something you can check. That can be a very good task for AI. And then you have something that seems like straightforward administrative work, but it involves five different systems, a bunch of unwritten rules, and knowing whom to ask when something goes wrong. That can be much harder.

So I’d look at a few things. Does the system have access to the context it needs? Can it take the actions it needs to take? And can you tell whether it succeeded? The workflows where those things are clear are much easier to automate.

There’s also a big difference between doing a task most of the time and owning the entire workflow. If you’re helping a person, they can catch mistakes and handle exceptions. If you’re automating it end to end, you have to deal with all those exceptions yourself. Often, that last piece is where a lot of the work is.

r001.rationale: The response describes self-contained tasks as easier, but does not identify highly scripted workflows or regulated industries.

r002.rationale: It notes that unwritten rules make some work harder and that clear workflows are easier, but does not state that less scripted work first requires making the process explicit.

r003.rationale: It mentions complex work spanning systems and unwritten rules, but does not explain that workers may struggle to describe one workflow because their jobs do not follow one.
